newsitem.title: THAILAND: Burma calls on ASEAN to resist pressure from U.S.
newsitem.headline: Burma calls on ASEAN to resist pressure from U.S.

text.p: Burma on Saturday urged its neighbours to resist pressure by the United States aimed at preventing Rangoon's entry into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) this year.

"ASEAN will have to stick to its guns to show that nobody dictates to us," a government official told Reuters in a telephone interview from Rangoon. "Generally we believe if ASEAN gives in this time then ASEAN will have to give in every time."

He was responding to remarks made in Washington on Friday by U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, who said the United States was lobbying members of ASEAN not to admit Burma to the seven-member regional grouping this year.

"We don't believe that ASEAN should take this step," Burns said. "We're trying to use our influence with the ASEAN partners to make the point that Burma should be given a stiff message that it's not welcome."
The Burmese official said he was not surprised the United States was lobbying ASEAN -- which comprises Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
"I knew of course that they were going to try to increase the pressure," the government official said. "We have said they would put more and more pressure on Myanmar (Burma)."
"ASEAN countries have seen through the pretext the United States has been using. They have realised it's not democracy the United States wants to impose here, it's hypocrisy," he said.

The United States last week banned new American investment in Burma as a condemnation of the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council's (SLORC's) alleged human rights abuses and its repression of the democracy movement led by Nobel Peace laureate Aung San Suu Kyi.
Burns' comments on Friday appeared to step up long-standing Western unhappiness about ASEAN's plan to admit Burma.

The U.S. charge d'affaires in Burma, Kent Wiedemann, had said in an interview on Thursday that while Washington would find it "awkward" to deal with an ASEAN that included Burma its admission was "something ASEAN has to decide for itself."

Western nations argue that Burma's admission to ASEAN would be tantamount to approval of the military regime's rights abuses and its failure to recognise the 1990 victory of the National League for Democracy, which was co-founded by Suu Kyi.

"Burma's human rights performance is so woeful, so irresponsible, that surely it should not be treated as a normal country and should not be rewarded by membership in one of the most prestigious and important pan-Asian organisations, with which the United States is affiliated," Burns said.

ASEAN, which follows a policy of "constructive engagement" towards Burma in the thought that isolation can only make things worse, is expected to admit observer nations Burma, Cambodia and Laos as full members this year.
Leaders of ASEAN member nations said last week the U.S. sanctions would not impact Burma's entry to the grouping.
